title: Styrene and HBr
subtitle: A benzylic cation, stabilised by the ring

reactants.caption: styrene + hydrogen bromide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Styrene reacts with HBr. Draw the protonation.
hintTiers: Which π bond reacts: the ring or the side-chain C=C? Which end gets the proton?
The side-chain π bond takes the proton at the CH₂ end, so the positive charge lands next to the ring. The H–Br bond breaks onto bromine. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from the side-chain C=C π bond to the H, forming a bond from the CH₂ carbon to H. Arrow 2: from the H–Br bond onto bromine.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That leaves a primary cation on the end carbon, not conjugated with the ring. Put the H on the CH₂ end so the positive charge sits next to the ring.
Using a ring π bond would destroy aromaticity. The side-chain alkene is far more reactive.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start. Hydrogen can only have one bond: break the H–Br bond onto bromine.

benzylic-cation.caption: benzylic cation + bromide
benzylic-cation.learnerPrompt: Why is this cation so stable? Draw a resonance form with the positive charge in the ring.
hintTiers: The cationic carbon is next to a ring π bond. Which way can those electrons move?
Move the ring π bond that touches the side chain to between the ring carbon and the cationic carbon. One arrow.
From the ring C=C π bond next to the side chain to between the ring carbon and the cationic carbon. The charge moves onto the ortho carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: There is no positive charge on that ring carbon in this drawing.

ring-cation-form.caption: a resonance form of the benzylic cation: positive charge on an ortho carbon
ring-cation-form.learnerPrompt: Now let bromide add. Where does it go?
hintTiers: Bromide could add where any resonance form puts the positive charge. Which choice keeps the ring aromatic?
Bromide adds to the benzylic carbon (outside the ring), and the side-chain π bond moves back into the ring. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from a bromide lone pair to the benzylic carbon. Arrow 2: from the exocyclic C=C π bond to between the ring carbon and the positively charged ortho carbon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Adding to the ring carbon would leave a non-aromatic ring. Bromide adds to the benzylic carbon, and the ring becomes aromatic again.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right place. That carbon would now have five bonds: move its C=C π bond back into the ring.

steps.explanationAfterStep: A secondary benzylic cation: the empty p orbital overlaps with the ring π system.
A resonance form, not a new species. The charge is spread over the benzylic carbon and the ortho and para ring carbons.
Bromide adds at the benzylic carbon, the one position that leaves the ring aromatic.
Also correct: bromide adds straight to the benzylic cation. The resonance form only shows why this cation forms so easily.

mechanismSummary: Protonation at the CH₂ end of styrene gives a benzylic cation: the positive charge is shared with the ring. Bromide adds at the benzylic carbon, so the ring stays aromatic: (1-bromoethyl)benzene.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 20
